title: If you can’t explain it simply...
author: Lee LeFever
summary: Lee LeFever takes the saying often attributed to Einstein, that if you cannot explain something simply you do not understand it well enough, and asks what understanding actually consists of. He proposes his own four-part framework, framed as questions: what is it, why does it work as it does, where else does this work, and what does it help me do. He illustrates each with a bicycle and its chain, extending to a garage door opener, and then tests the framework on interpreting his dog Piper's whining at the door. The move of the piece is to connect understanding to explanation: the four questions expose gaps in the explainer's own understanding and also help diagnose what a particular audience is missing. LeFever notes that a useful explanation need not answer all four questions, only the one the audience lacks. He closes by inviting readers to apply the framework to a subject of their own.
points: LeFever defines understanding through four questions covering identity, mechanism, transfer to other cases, and practical application.
The bicycle-to-garage-door example shows how grasping a mechanism lets understanding transfer to a new situation.
The dog example demonstrates that meaning comes from context, and that understanding lets one form and test predictions.
He argues that the same questions help an explainer diagnose which part of a concept a given audience is actually missing.
quotes: Like all things regarding the mind, there is hidden complexity because you can't see understanding happen. It's a very personal phenomenon.
You should be able to identify it. You should recognize it and distinguish what makes it unique among similar items.
You should be able to apply your understanding to other examples and explain what they have in common. By understanding a bike, you can explain a garage door opener in similar terms
If you observe that the pedals turn, but they don't drive the back wheel, you know to check the chain. Your understanding of the system helped you see a missing connection.
Here we see that Piper's whine alone doesn't tell me exactly what she needs. The meaning comes from the situation and context, which help me interpret her whining and take action.
This relates to a fundamental idea in communication: you, the explainer, must understand the subject yourself. The four questions above can expose what parts of the subject you don't yet understand.
Further, the four questions can help you evaluate what needs to be explained. A useful explanation doesn't have to answer all four.
